```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# Show stores below the temporary folder as `<tempdir>/...`, use UTC and a
# fixed width so that the output is the same on every machine.
local({
  dirs <- unique(c(
    normalizePath(tempdir(), winslash = "/", mustWork = FALSE),
    normalizePath(tempdir(), winslash = "\\", mustWork = FALSE),
    tempdir()
  ))
  hide <- function(x) {
    for (d in dirs) x <- gsub(d, "<tempdir>", x, fixed = TRUE)
    x
  }
  for (h in c("output", "message", "warning", "error")) {
    old <- knitr::knit_hooks$get(h)
    knitr::knit_hooks$set(stats::setNames(
      list(local({
        old <- old
        function(x, options) old(hide(x), options)
      })),
      h
    ))
  }
})
old_options <- options(width = 80, cli.width = 120, cli.hyperlink = FALSE)
old_tz <- Sys.getenv("TZ", unset = NA)
Sys.setenv(TZ = "UTC")
```

rcs keeps tabular, geospatial vector and raster data in a *store*: a named
collection of *datasets*, written mostly as Parquet files. This vignette
works with a store in one local folder. It shows how to create the store,
write a table, see what the store holds, open a dataset and read part of it
back, and keep earlier versions.

The way to work with a dataset is `store_open()`: it opens the dataset
lazily, without reading it, you describe the rows you want with dplyr
verbs, and `collect()` reads them into R.

Three other vignettes go further: `vignette("locations")` keeps the same
store in several places, local folders or cloud buckets,
`vignette("geospatial")` writes `sf` objects and rasters, and
`vignette("duckdb")` queries a store with DuckDB.

```{r setup}
library(rcs)
```

## Words used here

- A **store** is a collection of datasets, whatever the place it is kept in.
- A **location** is one place that holds a copy of a store: a local folder,
  or a Google Cloud Storage address such as `gs://my-bucket/store`.
- The **catalog** is a set of three small Parquet files at the root of each
  location. It lists every dataset and every data file, with checksums.
  Every function starts from the catalog; folders are never searched for
  files.
- A **dataset** is one logical table, named like a path: `sales/daily`. It
  is stored as one file, or as one file per *partition* (for example one per
  year).
- A **version** is a 16-character code computed from the content of a
  dataset's files. Each file also embeds the dataset's metadata: its name,
  title, description, key, partition and column types, among others. So
  the same rows give the same version only with the same name and the
  same metadata; a change of title alone gives a new version.

## Create a store

`store_connect()` connects to a store and returns a connection object.
With `create = TRUE`, a folder that holds no store yet is set up with empty
catalogs. Here the store lives in the session's temporary folder.

```{r}
path <- file.path(tempdir(), "my-store")
st <- store_connect(path, create = TRUE)
st
```

`store_create(path)` does the same set-up without connecting. Use it once,
when a store is new; connect with `store_connect(path)` afterwards.

## Write a table

The package ships generators of simulated data for examples.
`rcs_sim_table()` returns a panel of invented daily sales, with a column of
almost every R type: integers, doubles, dates, factors, 64-bit integers,
time differences, text with accents, list columns and times.

```{r}
sales <- rcs_sim_table(300, seed = 1)
sales
```

`store_write()` writes a data frame as one dataset. A title and a
description are required. `key` names the columns that identify a row: their
values must be unique together, and the write stops if they are not.
`partition` writes one file per value of the named columns.

```{r}
store_write(st, sales, "sales/daily",
  title = "Daily sales",
  description = "Simulated daily sales by shop and product.",
  key = c("shop_id", "date", "product"),
  partition = "year"
)
```

The summary says what was written and where. Before anything is copied to
the store, the files are written to a local staging folder and a sample of
their rows is compared with `sales`. After the copy, the checksum (MD5) of
every file in the store is compared with the staged one. Only then is the
catalog switched to the new version, so a reader never sees a half-written
dataset.

A dataset that exists is written again only with `mode = "replace"` or
`mode = "update"`. With the default `mode = "create"`, the write stops with
an error (class `rcs_error_dataset_exists`). If the new data and metadata
give the version the store already holds, nothing is uploaded and the
summary says the dataset is unchanged. That is the case here:

```{r}
store_write(st, sales, "sales/daily",
  title = "Daily sales",
  description = "Simulated daily sales by shop and product.",
  key = c("shop_id", "date", "product"),
  partition = "year",
  mode = "replace"
)
```

## See what the store holds

Printing the connection lists its locations and its datasets, grouped by
folder.

```{r}
st
```

`store_datasets()` returns the same list as a tibble, one row per dataset.

```{r}
datasets <- store_datasets(st)
datasets
datasets$title
```

`store_describe()` shows everything the catalog knows about one dataset:
title, description, key, partition, the columns with their types, and the
files of the current version.

```{r}
store_describe(st, "sales/daily")
```

These three functions read only the catalog that the connection holds. They
open no data file, so they are fast also for a store in a cloud bucket.

A dataset can be named by the last part of its name when that is unique in
the store: `"daily"` stands for `"sales/daily"` below.

## Open a dataset

`store_open()` opens a dataset as a lazy query. It reads no data: the query
is built from the files the catalog names. Printing it shows a header and
the first rows.

```{r}
q <- store_open(st, "daily")
q
```

The header says what the query reads:

- `Dataset:` the full name, the number of rows and columns, and the kind.
  The number of rows comes from the catalog; it is known as long as the
  query is the whole dataset, with columns at most selected, renamed or
  computed.
- `Location:` the location read, here the primary, a local folder.
- `Version:` the first characters of the version, and whether it is the
  current one.
- `Files:` how many of the dataset's files the query reads.

Printing reads the rows it shows, and no more. It shows 10 rows, or `n`;
the option `rcs.print_rows` changes the default.

```{r}
print(q, n = 3)
```

The query is changed with the dplyr verbs `filter()`, `select()`,
`mutate()`, `rename()`, `arrange()`, `distinct()` and `head()`. Each verb
returns a new query; still nothing is read.

```{r}
q24 <- q |>
  dplyr::filter(year == 2024, qty > 45) |>
  dplyr::select(shop_id, date, product, qty)
q24
```

After a filter the number of rows is not known without reading, so the
header shows `??`. `Files: 1 of 2 (pruned)` says that one file is enough:
a filter on the partition columns alone is first applied to the catalog,
and only the files of the matching partitions are opened. `Filter:` shows
the row filter that is passed to the Parquet reader.

`collect()` runs the query and returns a tibble.

```{r}
q24 |>
  dplyr::mutate(big_day = qty > 48) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(qty)) |>
  dplyr::collect()
```

Filters and the column selection are passed to the Parquet reader, so only
the needed files, blocks of rows and columns are read. The work counters
show it: with `options(rcs.trace = TRUE)`, `rcs_trace()` reports the work
done by the last call.

```{r}
options(rcs.trace = TRUE)
x <- q |> dplyr::filter(year == 2023) |> dplyr::collect()
rcs_trace()[c("counter", "detail", "n")]
options(rcs.trace = FALSE)
```

One of the two files was opened. The records are kept until the next call
of a package function; `rcs_trace_reset()` clears them.

## Read in one call

`store_read()` is the shortcut for `store_open()`, `filter()`, `select()`
and `collect()` in one call. Filters are written as in `dplyr::filter()`,
and `columns` selects columns as in `dplyr::select()`.

```{r}
store_read(st, "daily", year == 2024, product == "p07",
  columns = c(shop_id, date, qty)
)
```

The types of the columns come back as they were written: factor levels,
64-bit integers, time differences with their units, list columns and time
zones included. Rows come back sorted by the key within each partition,
so both sides are sorted before they are compared.

```{r}
back <- store_read(st, "daily")
identical(
  dplyr::arrange(sales, shop_id, date, product),
  dplyr::arrange(back, shop_id, date, product)
)
```

Two functions give a first look without reading a whole dataset.
`store_glimpse()` prints the catalog facts and the first rows of one file.
`store_sample()` draws rows from a few randomly chosen blocks of rows. It is
a quick way to look at the data, not a simple random sample: rows of one
block are alike, because rows are stored sorted.

```{r}
store_glimpse(st, "daily")
store_sample(st, "daily", n = 5, qty > 40, columns = c(shop_id, date, qty),
  seed = 42
)
```

## Update some partitions

With `mode = "update"`, only the partitions whose values occur in the new
data are replaced; the other partitions stay as they are. It works only on
a partitioned dataset: a dataset stored as one file must be written with
`mode = "replace"`. Here the rows of 2024 are written again with corrected
quantities. The key, the partition columns and the column types come from
the stored dataset and must match.

```{r}
fix <- sales[sales$year == 2024, ]
fix$qty <- fix$qty + 1L
store_write(st, fix, "sales/daily",
  title = "Daily sales",
  description = "Simulated daily sales by shop and product.",
  mode = "update"
)
```

The message lists every replaced partition with its old and new number of
rows. Check it: a row of a replaced partition that is missing from the new
data is gone after the update.

## Keep earlier versions

By default a store keeps only the current version of each dataset: the
files of a replaced version are deleted once the catalog points to the new
ones. A store created with `history = TRUE` keeps them. The setting can
also be given for one connection (`store_connect(history = )`) or one
dataset (`store_write(history = )`); the dataset's setting wins over the
connection's, and the connection's over the store's.

```{r}
path_h <- file.path(tempdir(), "store-with-history")
store_create(path_h, history = TRUE)
sth <- store_connect(path_h)

store_write(sth, sales, "sales/daily",
  title = "Daily sales",
  description = "Simulated daily sales by shop and product.",
  key = c("shop_id", "date", "product"),
  partition = "year"
)
store_write(sth, fix, "sales/daily",
  title = "Daily sales",
  description = "Simulated daily sales by shop and product.",
  mode = "update"
)
```

`store_history()` lists the versions, the current one first.

```{r}
versions <- store_history(sth, "daily")
versions[c("version", "current", "n_files", "rows", "complete")]
```

An earlier version is read by its code:

```{r}
first <- versions$version[!versions$current][1]
store_read(sth, "daily", year == 2024, columns = c(shop_id, date, qty),
  version = first
) |>
  head(3)
```

Old versions stay until `store_prune()` removes them. `keep` is the number
of earlier versions to keep; `dry_run = TRUE` only reports. Files that the
current version still uses are never deleted. The count of files covers
data files and the manifest of each removed version. Here the update
replaced one partition, so the old version leaves one data file and one
manifest.

```{r}
store_prune(sth, keep = 0, dry_run = TRUE)
store_prune(sth, keep = 0)
```

## Check a dataset

`store_check()` without data checks the integrity of a stored dataset:
every file exists with the checksum and the number of rows its catalog
records, and the catalog agrees with itself. Given the data the dataset was
written from, it compares a sample of stored rows with them. In a store
with several locations, `locations` limits the check to some of them (see
`vignette("locations")`).

```{r}
store_check(st, "daily")
store_check(sth, "daily", x = rbind(sales[sales$year != 2024, ], fix))
```

Both return a tibble of results invisibly, and stop with an error when a
check fails (`error = FALSE` only reports).

```{r, include = FALSE}
unlink(c(path, path_h), recursive = TRUE)
options(old_options)
if (is.na(old_tz)) Sys.unsetenv("TZ") else Sys.setenv(TZ = old_tz)
```
